opening.headline: When you need to collect data, ask questions, and conduct web research, you will learn how to divide Claude's Projects and Research into internal and external data.
body: PDFs of contracts, meeting minutes, and reports are scattered all over the place, and questions are asked repeatedly about the same materials. At the same time, you should search the web for the latest news from your competitors. If you have a question that needs to be answered within your data and something you need to find outside, it becomes difficult to know which tool to use.

In this class, we will look at the composition and disclosure scope of Projects that contain materials as knowledge files. Next, we compare which questions web search, expanded thinking, and research are appropriate for, and explain examples of deploying these functions in competitor analysis work.
objectives: Can explain the role of Projects and Research
Can distinguish between web search, expanded thinking, and research selection criteria
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

screens.title: It is necessary to collect data and conduct web research.
screens.lead: Let's look at two types of demands mixed in one task. When you select each item, an explanation will unfold.

items.answer: PDFs of contracts, meeting minutes, and reports are scattered across folders, and questions are asked about the same materials over and over again. It takes time to upload and explain files every time.

items.prompt: What's out there: Latest news from competitors
items.answer: Competitors' prices and new features aren't anywhere in my documentation, so I have to look them up on the web. This is something I cannot answer with just my data.

items.prompt: What happens when these two are mixed in one question?
items.answer: One sentence, ‘Compare our product with our competitors’ contains both the part to be answered with my own data and the part to be brought in from outside. If you don't decide which tool is responsible for which part, you'll end up having to paste data every time or write out-of-date information.

items.prompt: So what are the questions in this lesson?
items.answer: The first step is to determine whether the answer to my question is within or outside of my data. The inside is handled by Projects' knowledge files, and the outside is handled by web searches and research.

screens.outro: First, let's think about how we are currently handling the material.

screens.title: Think about it: When combining data collection and web research
screens.lead: Read the questions and think for yourself first. There is no need to submit an answer, and when you select an item, the instructor's thoughts unfold.

items.prompt: What tools do you use when collecting data and conducting web research simultaneously?
items.answer: It is common to collect documents in folders, conduct web research separately using a search engine, and then organize the results by putting them in one place. Because the tools are divided, you constantly need to copy and paste between them.

items.prompt: Aren't you pasting the data every time now?
items.answer: If you're pasting the same document every time you open a new conversation, it's better to upload that material once into a knowledge file. It is efficient to keep repetitive material in one place and write multiple conversations together.

items.prompt: How deep should your web research be?
items.answer: Checking a single price and synthesizing trends from multiple competitors with sources are two completely different things. In this lesson, you will see that the correct function varies depending on the depth.

screens.outro: Now let’s take a look at the configuration of Projects.

screens.title: Projects: Workspace with knowledge files
screens.lead: Select the two states alternately to compare when using without a project and when using with a project.

visual.alt: Mockup showing the knowledge area, chat list, and share buttons on the project screen.

states.label: without project
states.body: In general chat, data is posted in each conversation. Opening a new conversation will not carry over the context of the previous conversation, so you will have to re-upload the same document and provide the same explanation again. Chats have an upload limit of 500MB per file and 20 per chat. In tasks that require reference to the same material across multiple conversations, this repetition becomes a huge burden.

states.label: in project
states.body: Projects is an independent workspace with its own chat history and knowledge base. In Projects, click + New Project to create a name and description. This name and description will not be visible to Claude. When you post documents, text files, or code to a project's knowledge area, all chats in that project use that material as context. You can set instructions on how Claude will answer in Set project instructions, and in the paid plan, when knowledge approaches the context window limit, RAG mode is automatically turned on to increase capacity. However, chats within a project do not share context unless information is included in the knowledge base. Free accounts can create up to 5 projects. In Team and Enterprise, you can keep it private or make it visible to the entire organization. Even if it is public, your chats within the project are private unless you share them separately.

screens.outro: Now that we know how to store our data, let's compare three ways to handle external information.

screens.title: Selection Criteria for Web Search, Expanding Thinking, and Research
screens.lead: Select each tab to find out which questions the three features are suitable for and how they work together.

tabs.label: web search
tabs.body: Web searches are great for simple fact-checking that can be accomplished with one or two tool calls. Examples include questions such as checking the weather, information about a specific company, recent news headlines, or last night's game results. It's also great if you want to give a rough guide on what to search for, but leave the actual search and result analysis to Claude. All responses are accompanied by citations so you can directly check the source.

tabs.label: Turn on web browsing
tabs.body: When you select Web search from the + button at the bottom left of the dialog window, it turns on and a check mark appears. You can turn it off by pressing it again. The new Claude experience lets Claude search the web when it helps, without any separate switches. In Team and Enterprise accounts, the owner must first turn on web browsing in Capabilities in Organization Settings before members can use it. If web search is turned on, web fetching, which directly retrieves page content when a URL is given, is also possible, and if you retrieve an entire long article, your Free account can use up a lot of usage.

tabs.label: expansion thinking
tabs.body: Expansive thinking shines in complex reasoning that doesn't require up-to-date information. Examples include solving math problems, debugging code, and analyzing philosophical concepts, and are suitable for questions that need to be considered from multiple angles, such as 'Improve the performance of an algorithm.' Use it alone when you want Claude to think more deeply and find an answer without searching the web or using the integration.

tabs.label: Research
tabs.body: Research is suitable for comprehensive information gathering that requires five or more tool calls and takes 1 to 3 minutes. Create in-depth reports by combining multiple sources from across the web and integrations. Examples include comparing competitors, updating old internal documents with web information, and setting priorities and tasks in calendars and emails. Produce a lengthy final report that synthesizes multiple sources with citations.

tabs.label: write together
tabs.body: Together, Expanded Thinking and Research allow you to carefully plan your approach and execute comprehensive information gathering. Examples include researching a new technology, writing a business proposal, or analyzing several scientific papers. Depending on the depth of your question, decide whether to write them alone or in combination.

screens.outro: Once standards are written, tasks can be divided into one task. Let’s check with an example.

screens.title: Narrative Case Study: Competitor Analysis
screens.lead: The instructor will demonstrate the process of deploying capabilities in a competitive analysis task. Select the next arrow to follow the steps.

steps.title: read request
steps.body: The request is ‘a report comparing our product with three of our competitors’. In this one sentence, you'll get something from your source (your product description) and something from outside (your competitors' prices, features, trends). Therefore, rather than handling it with one tool, the functions are divided up.

steps.title: Step 1: My materials into project knowledge files
steps.body: Our product documentation and internal meeting minutes are posted to the project knowledge file. All chats in that project will then answer based on the same data. The project guidelines note the format and comparison items for the report. The project name and description are invisible to Claude, so the content of the material is placed in the knowledge area, not the name.

steps.title: Step 2: A web search for facts
steps.body: Checking one competitor's latest price is a fact-check that can be accomplished with one or two tool calls. Web search is fine. It is sufficient to open the citation attached to the response and verify that the source is correct.

steps.title: Step 3: External synthesis into research
steps.body: Compiling and citing the characteristics and trends of the three competitors requires multiple tool calls and multiple sources. This is an area where Research is a good fit and returns lengthy reports with citations. Web searches yield more consistent results than asking one question at a time. If there is a linked app, Research can use the web and the source of the linked function, making it suitable for updating internal documents with web information.

steps.title: Step 4: Refine logic with expanded thinking
steps.body: If the report is long and complex and the logic of comparison needs to be refined, expand thinking is added. It can help you consider in depth what criteria the comparison is based on and whether the conclusion is consistent with the evidence. This function is used when inference, not the latest information, is the key.

steps.title: Step 5: Decide on privacy
steps.body: In Team or Enterprise, you can keep projects private or open to the entire organization. If you want to view the comparison report with your team, it is safe to share privately with only those who need it, and you can change the visibility at any time. Even if it is a public project, your chats are private unless you share them separately. When sharing, each member chooses the level they need between view-only and broader permissions. If you don't see Web Search, check to see if the owner needs to turn it on in your organization settings first. In addition, in some cases, project sharing itself has been turned off by the administrator, so if you do not see the sharing button, check the organization's project sharing settings as well.

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: The layout of this case is summarized in one line: The material inside is Projects, the short facts outside are web searches, the long synthesis outside is Research, and the deep reasoning is expanded thinking. For each question, the function is determined by first asking whether the answer is inside or outside, short or long.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the role of each function in the examples, we will summarize the lesson.

screens.title: Organization: data inside and data outside
screens.lead: Let's summarize what we've seen so far. Read while remembering whether the answer to your question is within or without.

paragraphs: The project stores my data as a knowledge file and uses it in all chats of the project. The project name and description are invisible to Claude, so the context is placed in the knowledge area and project instructions. Also remember that chats on the same project do not share context other than what you put in the knowledge base.

The external information is divided according to the depth of the question. Web Search is suitable for short fact-checking, while Research is suitable for longer investigations that synthesize multiple sources. Expansive thinking is suitable for inferences that require deep consideration without up-to-date information, and can be used in conjunction with Research to enhance both planning and gathering.

Teams and Enterprise determine the visibility of projects, and web browsing must first be turned on by the owner in the organization settings. Even if it is a public project, your chats within the project are private unless you share them.
All results can be trusted only if you make it a habit to check them yourself by opening the citations and source links.

When you get a new question, ask three questions in order. Is the answer in my data, a short fact out there, or a long synthesis out there? This order determines one of Projects, Web Search, and Research.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: The project name and description are not visible to Claude. The information Claude needs to know should be included in the knowledge domain or project instructions.

glossary.def: An independent workspaces with its own chat history and knowledge base.
This is a document, text, or code that is posted in the project knowledge area and referenced by all chats in that project.
A feature that combines sources from various origins with web and linking capabilities through multiple tool invocations to generate a report with citations.
The ability to check facts and find the latest news with just one or two tool calls.
A feature that enables deeper investigation into complex issues without the latest information.

misconceptions.myth: Research is a quick version of a general search.
misconceptions.fact: Research is a comprehensive investigation that synthesizes information from multiple sources over a period of 1 to 3 minutes, using five or more tool calls, to produce a long report with cited references. Simple fact verification is better suited to web search.

misconceptions.myth: The project name and description are also referenced by Claude.
misconceptions.fact: The project's name and description are not visible to Claude. To make them accessible, they must be uploaded to the knowledge base or included in the project instructions.

misconceptions.myth: If it is a public project, the chat within it is also public.
misconceptions.fact: Even if the project is made public within the organization, members cannot see the private chat messages unless they are explicitly shared.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The project contains my own materials, while Research aggregates external materials.
Web searches are suitable for short fact-checking, and Research is suitable for long-term comprehensive research.
Expanded thinking is appropriate for inferences that require in-depth consideration without up-to-date information.
The project's public scope is defined by Team and Enterprise, and web access is initially enabled by the owner.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Is the answer to my question contained within my data, or outside of it? Is this question a brief confirmation, or a comprehensive analysis?

checks.q: How should Claude be configured to utilize our company's data in all chat sessions within the project?
options: Enter detailed content of the materials into the project name and description.
Upload documents to the project knowledge area
Turn on web browsing when starting each chat
Make the project public for your organization
checks.explain: Documents and text posted to the knowledge area are used in all chats for that project. The name and description are not visible to Claude.

wrong.0: The name and description are not visible to Claude, so they are not a means of conveying context.
wrong.2: Web search is a function to find external information.
wrong.3: The scope of disclosure determines who sees it and is different from the way Claude writes the material.

checks.intro: Find out how to make sure your project materials are available in every chat.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Articles posted in the knowledge area will be used in all chats for that project.
checks.incorrectFeedback: The project name and description are invisible to Claude. Materials must be posted in the knowledge area.

checks.q: Match the following situations with the appropriate choices:
left: Our product documentation and internal meeting minutes
Comprehensive trends from three competitors with sources
Thinking deeply about math problems without up-to-date information
checks.explain: The data inside is a project, the short facts outside are web searches, the long synthesis outside is research, and the deep reasoning is expanded thinking.
checks.intro: The appropriate choice will depend on the location of the material and the length of the task. Match situations and choices.
checks.correctFeedback: All are correct. You accurately distinguished between data on the inside, short facts on the outside, long synthesis on the outside, and deep reasoning.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatched pair. Internal data is Project, short up-to-date facts are Web searches, long syntheses that require sources are Research, and deep inferences that do not require up-to-date information are Extended Thinking.
